newsitem.title: USA: AT&T sees Q2 as EPS nadir, confident on Q3.
newsitem.headline: AT&T sees Q2 as EPS nadir, confident on Q3.

text.p: AT&T Corp said Monday the decline in its second quarter earnings was the low point for the company, and year-over-year comparisons should become more favorable in future quarters.

In a conference call with analysts and reporters, Dan Somers, AT&T's new chief financial officer, also said he was comfortable with the First Call consensus earnings estimate of $0.64 per share for the third quarter.
AT&T today reported earnings from continuing operations of $0.59 per share for the second quarter, down from $0.95 a year earlier.

AT&T warned in March that earnings for the second quarter, the rest of 1997 and into 1998 would be diluted by heavy investments it is making to strengthen its presence in high-growth markets like local service and wireless.

Somers said the company spent $2.5 billion in the first half of 1997 on its capital spending initiatives. He said he expects capital spending for the full year to be at the low end of the $8-$9 billion the company had projected.
Looking to 1998, Somers said AT&T was still developing its capital spending plans but that, "Assume we will be a little more difficult on capital spending going forward."
The CFO said the company had made substantial progress in holding the line on operating expenses, which grew only $15 million, or 1 percent, in the second quarter.
He said AT&T's selling, general and administrative expenses for the full 1997 year would be below the 1996 total of $14.8 billion.

Gail McGovern, head of AT&T's consumer markets business, who also participated in the conference call, said the company continued to make progress in shifting its new customer marketing to "free minutes" programs from costly one-time checks.

McGovern said check-writing to win new customers had dropped below 30 percent. A year ago, the company was writing checks of around $100 per household to acquire up to 60 percent of its new customers.
She said AT&T was on track to reach its goal of obtaining less than 20 percent of its new customers through such checks by the end of 1997.

Somers said that while second quarter consumer long distance revenues declined by 0.8 percent versus the same quarter a year ago, as much as two percentage points of the decline was related to the move from checks to free-minute giveways, which generate no revenue in themselves.

Somers said he believed second quarter results would prove to be the "low mark" in terms of year-over-year earnings declines and that future quarters would see improvement, beginning with the third quarter.
He said he was "confident" the company can meet Wall Street's consensus earnings estimate of $0.64 per share for the third quarter.
"We are not pleased with year-over-year earnings declines," Somers said. "Our priority is growth."
